main_text.p:
Cunċta putant agitare sortes.
Et fortuitis ductibus obsequi
Terras, & altos ætheris ardui
Tractus, & ignes, atque fluctus
Naufragos maris æstuosi.
Frustra lauantur fluminibus sues,
Semper salebras, semper amant lutum:
Ditéfque gemmas, atque plena
Despiciunt alabastra nardo.
Nec fas proterui res canibus sacras
Offerre. Cassis lumine quid iuuat
Monstrare Soles: atque surdo
Mellifluum recitare carmen?
Vos pura testor pectora: Vos, quibus
Cœlestis almas Lux Sapientiæ
Mentes serenat. Quos benignus
Seruat amor Superum parentis.
Fauete linguis. Discite ceu polo
Mens cunċta cernit prouida Cœlitum.
Et sola ceu totum potente
Arbitrio moderatur orbem.
Hoc æthra fulgens monstrat, & aureus
Titan, decorum seu reuehens diem
Caliginosas pellit umbras,
Et vegeto recreat virentes
Calore campos: tempora seu citis
Annósque signat cursibus impiger:
Candentis aut Lunæ propinquans

page.notes:
Verse lines are set as one paragraph per stanza-like run; line breaks shown with
. Long s is rendered as s throughout. The printed text reads "Cunċta" with a combining mark over the c in the scan's ligature-like form; "cunċta" and "cunċta" are the same word. Several words are slightly doubtful in the scan due to ink fading and uneven inking, notably "Cassis" and "Discite", but no [?] was needed on confident readings. "Mens cunċta" and "Nec fas proterui" are as printed (the printer's "proterui" is a spelling of protervi and is left as printed). The last line ends on "propinquans" and the text continues on the next page.
